segments.t: Art director Vika Goncharova steps into the chef's office to thank the new head chef, German Land. He recently took the blame for a prank and saved Vika from being fired by Dmitry Nagiyev. Let's listen to their polite exchange in Russian.
Let's go through Vika and German's conversation in the office line by line.
'Viktoriya Sergeyevna, come in, please.' German welcomes Vika into his office with a polite plural imperative and formal address.
'I wanted to thank you once again.' Vika uses a feminine past-tense verb of wishing followed by a perfective infinitive of gratitude.
'I want to say a big thank you to you.' She pairs a polite dative pronoun with the standard Russian expression for thanking someone.
'You saved me from being fired.' The perfective past verb takes an accusative personal pronoun and a genitive noun meaning dismissal.
'I do not know how to thank you.' An indirect question with an interrogative adverb and an imperfective infinitive expresses her sincere appreciation.
'Perhaps you will try this dessert?' German offers a culinary treat using a modal phrase meaning perhaps and a polite second-person plural verb.
'Did you prepare it yourself just now?' An emphatic plural pronoun highlights that the head chef made the dish personally.
'There is no need for any special gratitude.' A negative impersonal construction requires the genitive case on the feminine noun for gratitude.
'After all, you and I are friends.' Russian expresses 'you and I' naturally with a first-person plural inclusive phrase, softened by a conversational particle.
'Well, at least in the future.' A limiting particle meaning at least combines with a prepositional phrase meaning in prospect.
'I wish you bon appetit.' The traditional mealtime wish stands in the genitive case after an explicit verb of wishing.
'This looks simply delicious.' Vika compliments the presentation using a third-person singular verb and an adverb of taste. Now let's hear their office exchange again from beginning to end.

German charms Vika with a delicate dessert and hints that he hopes they will become more than colleagues. Notice the formal plural pronouns they use to maintain professional distance. See you in the next scene.
